items.question: What is the angle between the hands, in degrees?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $|30h - 5.5m|$, then take the smaller angle.

byKey.reflex: 245 is the long way round. Take $360 - 245 = 115$.
byKey.stuck: You left the hour hand on the 10. By 10:10 it has moved 5° on.

explain.text: $|30 \cdot 10 - 5.5 \cdot 10| = |300 - 55| = 245$, more than 180. So the angle is $360 - 245 = 115°$. Principle: take the smaller of the two angles.

items.prose: Only the last digit of 13 matters for the last digit of its powers.
items.question: What is the last digit of $13^{47}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the cycle of 3: 3, 9, 7, 1.

byKey.three: Remainder 1 gives 3. 47 leaves 3 on division by 4.

explain.text: $13^{47}$ ends like $3^{47}$, and the cycle 3, 9, 7, 1 has length 4. $47 = 4 \cdot 11 + 3$, so the last digit is the third, 7. Principle: drop all but the last digit, then use the cycle.

items.prose: Add the whole numbers from 1 to 300.
items.question: What is $1 + 2 + \cdots + 300$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Make 150 pairs that each add to 301.

byKey.whole: You forgot to halve. 300 numbers make 150 pairs.

explain.text: 1 with 300, 2 with 299 and so on make 150 pairs of 301. So the sum is $150 \times 301 = 45{,}150$. Principle: $\tfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$.

items.prose: Money grows at 4% a year, compounded yearly.
items.question: By the rule of 72, about how many years does it take to double?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 72 by the rate in per cent.

byKey.ln: $69.3/4 = 17.3$ is the small-rate rule. The question asks for the rule of 72.
byKey.simple: 25 years is simple interest, $100/4$. Compounding is faster.

explain.text: $72/4 = 18$ years, and the exact $\ln 2 / \ln 1.04 = 17.67$. At 4% the rule is a third of a year long. Principle: 72 fits best near 8%.

items.prose: You drive to a meeting at 45 km/h and back by the same road at 90 km/h.
items.question: What is your average speed for the round trip, in km/h?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the whole distance by the whole time.

byKey.mean: 67.5 is the plain mean. The slow leg takes twice as long.
byKey.sum: You added the speeds. The average must lie between them.

explain.text: Take 90 km each way: 2 hours out and 1 back, so 180 km in 3 hours. That is 60 km/h, or $\tfrac{2 \cdot 45 \cdot 90}{135}$. Principle: over equal distances, the harmonic mean.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the 5s at every layer: 5, 25 and 125.

byKey.once: 40 counts each multiple of 5 once. Multiples of 25 and 125 hold more.
byKey.two: You stopped at 25. 125 gives a third 5.

explain.text: $\lfloor 200/5 \rfloor + \lfloor 200/25 \rfloor + \lfloor 200/125 \rfloor = 40 + 8 + 1 = 49$. Each 5 meets a spare 2. Principle: count factors layer by layer.

items.question: What is the sum? Give a decimal or a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Only the first and last pieces survive.

byKey.start: You started at 1. The first term is $\tfrac{1}{3} - \tfrac{1}{4}$.
byKey.end: You kept $\tfrac{1}{3}$ and dropped the end. Subtract $\tfrac{1}{12}$.

explain.text: Each term is $\tfrac{1}{k} - \tfrac{1}{k+1}$, so the sum is $\tfrac{1}{3} - \tfrac{1}{12} = \tfrac{3}{12} = \tfrac{1}{4}$. Principle: write the term as a difference.

options.why: You used $2^{10} = 10^3$ and dropped the 2.4% excess. Over ten factors it grows to 27%.
$2^{10}$ is 1024, not 1000, so the two differ.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Carry the 2.4% excess through ten factors.

byKey.eq: 1024 is more than 1000, so its tenth power beats $1000^{10}$.

items.prose: Twenty people meet, and each pair shakes hands once.
items.question: How many handshakes are there?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count from each person, then halve.

byKey.twice: 380 counts each handshake from both people. Halve it.
byKey.square: 400 lets people shake their own hands and counts each handshake twice.

explain.text: Each of 20 people shakes 19 hands: 380 ends. Each handshake has two ends, so there are 190. Principle: $\binom{20}{2}$.

items.prose: A tap, a drain, a 5-litre jug and a 7-litre jug. A step fills a jug, empties one, or pours one into the other.
items.question: What is the fewest steps that leaves exactly 1 litre in a jug?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start by filling the 5-litre jug.

byKey.ten: 10 steps is the best start with the 7-litre jug. Starting with the 5-litre jug is shorter.
byKey.short: No 6-step route exists. Search every state to be sure.

explain.text: Fill 5, pour into 7, fill 5, pour (3, 7), empty 7, pour (0, 3), fill 5, pour: (1, 7). That is 8 steps, and a search finds none shorter. Principle: list states and search, as in Ropes, timers and jugs.
